t.3.33.1: Then, having heard those hair-raising words of Śūrpaṇakhā, he dismissed his ministers and, having resolved upon what was to be done, he departed.
t.3.33.2: Then, having pursued that matter and having understood it properly, and having weighed the strength and weakness of its faults and its merits,
t.3.33.4: Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, going in secret to the chariot-house, urged his charioteer, saying, "Let the chariot be yoked."
t.3.33.3: Having made up his own mind with the thought, “This is what must be done,” he, firm in resolve, then went to the delightful carriage-house.
t.3.33.5: Thus addressed, the swift-footed charioteer in an instant yoked the excellent chariot that was dear to him.
t.3.33.6: Mounting a golden chariot that moved at will and was adorned with jewels, yoked to donkeys with the faces of piśācas and decked with golden ornaments,
t.3.33.7: In that chariot, whose roar was like the thunder of clouds, the glorious lord of the rākṣasas, the younger brother of Dhanada, went to the ocean, the lord of rivers and streams.
t.3.33.9: Ten-faced and twenty-armed, with splendid attire and attendants, the foe of the thirty gods and slayer of the foremost sages, ten-headed, he stood like a king of mountains.
t.3.33.8: That ten-faced Daśānana, fanned with white yak-tail whisks and shaded by a white parasol, gleamed like glossy lapis lazuli and was adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
t.3.33.10: Having mounted his chariot that moved at will, the lord of the rākṣasas shone like a cloud in the sky, wreathed with flashes of lightning and accompanied by a line of cranes.
t.3.33.11: The mighty one gazed upon the marshy seacoast with its mountains, strewn everywhere with thousands of trees bearing many kinds of flowers and fruits.
t.3.33.12: It was surrounded on all sides by lotus ponds with cool and auspicious waters, and by spacious hermitage grounds furnished with sacrificial altars.
t.3.33.13: He beheld it crowded with plantains and āḍhakī shrubs and adorned with coconut palms, with sāla, palmyra and tamāla trees, and with other trees in full bloom.
t.3.33.14: It was graced by supreme seers who kept a strictly restrained diet, and by Nāgas, Suparṇas, Gandharvas and Kiṃnaras in their thousands.
t.3.33.15: It was adorned by those who had conquered desire, by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and by the Ājas, Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas and Marīcipas.
t.3.33.16: He was surrounded by apsarases in their thousands, wearing celestial ornaments and garlands, divine in form, and skilled in the arts of play and love.
t.3.33.17: It was frequented by the glorious wives of the gods and wrapped in splendor, and it was roamed by hosts of Devas and Dānavas, who feed on amṛta.
t.3.33.19: All around were celestial chariots, white and spacious, adorned with heavenly garlands and resounding with the music of instruments and song.
t.3.33.18: It was crowded with haṃsas, krauñcas and plavas and echoed with the cries of sārasa cranes; delightful, paved with stones of beryl, it glistened with the splendour of the ocean.
t.3.33.20: The cars of those who had won the heavenly worlds by their austerities, moving wherever they wished, were flying all around; and the younger brother of Dhanada also saw Gandharvas and Apsarases.
t.3.33.21: He saw, by the thousands, pleasant forests of sandalwood trees whose roots were moist with sap, forests that delighted the sense of smell.
t.3.33.22: He saw forests and groves of the finest agaru trees, of choice takkola trees, and of fragrant fruits.
t.3.33.23: The blossoms of the tamāla, the thickets of pepper, and the heaps of pearls lying out to dry along the shore.
t.3.33.24: He saw beds of conch shells and likewise heaps of coral, and everywhere golden and silver rocks.
t.3.33.25: There were charming springs and clear pools, and places rich in wealth and grain, filled with women who were jewels among their kind.
t.3.33.26: Gazing upon cities crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, he came upon that land, level on every side and lush, where the breezes were soft to the touch.
t.3.33.27: He beheld the watery coastland of the lord of rivers, which was like heaven, and there he saw a banyan tree, dark as a cloud, surrounded by sages.
t.3.33.28: It was the tree whose branches stretched out on every side for a hundred yojanas, and to whose branch the mighty Garuḍa came, carrying an elephant and a huge-bodied tortoise, in order to eat them.
t.3.33.29: Then Suparṇa, the best of birds, of mighty strength, suddenly broke that leafy branch of the tree with his weight.
t.3.33.30: There the supreme seers were gathered together: the Vaikhānasas, the Māṣas, the Vālakhilyas, the Marīcipas, the Ajas and the Dhūmras.
t.3.33.31: Out of compassion for them, Garuḍa swiftly took up that branch, a hundred yojanas long, together with both the elephant and the tortoise, and flew away.
t.3.33.33: With his prowess doubled by that very delight, the wise one resolved to bring back the amṛta.
t.3.33.32: With one foot the righteous best of birds devoured that flesh; then, having destroyed the land of the Niṣādas with the branch and set free the great sages, he attained incomparable joy.
t.3.33.34: Having crushed the nets of iron and broken open the excellent jewelled chamber, he then carried off the amṛta that was guarded in the palace of the great Indra.
t.3.33.35: The younger brother of Dhanada saw that banyan tree named Subhadra, frequented by hosts of great sages and bearing the marks made by Suparṇa.
t.3.33.36: Having reached that farther shore of the ocean, the lord of rivers, he saw a hermitage in a secluded spot within a holy and delightful stretch of forest.
t.3.33.37: There he saw the rākṣasa named Mārīca, wearing a black antelope skin, bearing matted locks and bark garments, and restrained in his diet.
t.3.33.38: That Rāvaṇa, skilled in speech, having met with that rākṣasa in due form, then afterwards spoke these words.
